How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

Concerns about AI are legitimate. These systems can be used to intensify surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate cyberattacks, and concentrate economic and political power. More capable systems may introduce additional risks, particularly when deployed without adequate testing or oversight.

We should not dismiss these dangers. But neither should we treat catastrophe as inevitable simply because a technology is powerful.

The answer to risk is not blind faith. It is serious evaluation, independent testing, appropriate safeguards, accountability, and governance proportionate to the potential harm. High-risk applications warrant greater scrutiny than routine uses.

I think the current transformer attention method is not the method to reach ASI. There will need to be something else that pushes it forward. From my understanding the large data corpus is really just an advanced prediction system. Something will need to come along to actually understand concepts terms and know how to reason about things.

I think there's an element of expressing our values, even in the face of technological uncertainty, that this story gets at. We can still decide as a society that this handful of companies must develop their tech on terms defined by the rest of us. They may seem powerful and they are certainly telling us they intend to be even more powerful, but that's not the same as having political power today. I like Newport's idea that everyone else's voices matter, too.

#3187. FT, NYT tie Alice Huang’s chip network to gaming tycoons and PLA suppliers

The Alice Huang chip network ran through hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Prince Group figure, the FT says. The NYT traces $3.6bn of Chinese state money to firms tied to her family.

Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California

Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Together they formed a network that supplied Nvidia chips to China. A day earlier, The New York Times tied companies linked to her family to suppliers of China’s military.

TNW has not independently verified either report. US officials suspect Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, the Times first reported in October, describing a Chinese spy plot. Beijing calls the claim a smear. Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November after admitting an affair with her. They are not related.

The FT’s Zijing Wu and Haohsiang Ko traced the Alice Huang chip network through hundreds of filings and more than a dozen sources. Its companies made billions moving Nvidia chips into China, not necessarily aware of the full picture, the paper reported.

It started with Inspur, one of Nvidia’s largest server partners in China. The US put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023, but not its part-owned US unit. Renamed Aivres, that unit kept trading with Nvidia. Inside Nvidia there were questions over whether it should count as a partner, a person with direct knowledge told the FT. Nvidia concluded that it met all compliance and export control rules.

Some of Inspur’s Chinese clients then turned to Century Huatong, an online gaming group turned data centre investor. The answer, people familiar with the plan said, was an offshore shell branded as a “neocloud”. That shell became Megaspeed, with Huang as its trusted public face.

Kang Wei, whom the FT calls her husband and the Times her business partner, was an early investor in Century Huatong, filings show. Megaspeed grew out of the Singapore arm of 7Road, a gaming firm that Huang and Century Huatong both backed. Its Malaysian unit, Speedmatrix, declared about $4.6bn of imports from Aivres in the year to December 2025. The FT cites ImportGenius trade data.

The last step was smuggling the chips into China. Hu Xiaowei filled at least part of that role, people familiar with the matter told the FT. US authorities call Hu the “second-in-command” at Prince Group. The US Treasury has named the group a transnational criminal organisation. Hu was arrested in Japan this summer.

A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu never worked for the business and called the US allegations unsupported. The FT could not reach Hu.

Nvidia said it put Megaspeed and a subsidiary on its block list in 2025 and has also restricted sales to Aivres. Megaspeed has said it runs a lawful business, and that Huang left in August 2025. Tencent, which owns 10.1% of Century Huatong, said it knew nothing of the activities. The FT found no evidence that Tencent or Alibaba took part.

The Times reviewed a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an intelligence firm staffed by former intelligence officers. About $3.6bn of Chinese state money flowed through companies tied to Huang’s family or associates, it found. The money funded projects including data centres with Nvidia chips. The Times said it confirmed many of the ties itself.

Most links are indirect, the Times said, and it is unclear whether the military used any of the computing power. The paper had already reported that Megaspeed’s backer Alibaba co-founded a military-linked lab.

“Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it,” Strider’s chief executive, Greg Levesque, told the Times.

Both papers point to Century Litong, a Shanghai firm founded by Century Longteng. The FT says Longteng was a venture between Century Huatong and a vehicle Huang controlled with her sister. The Times names the sister’s firm.

Century Litong was a key distributor of smuggled Nvidia chips in China, people with knowledge of the deals told the FT. The Information first reported its role. Its owner, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, also controls a maker of Chinese radar and missile parts, the Times reported.

Nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to Century Litong’s Hong Kong unit, licence files released on Thursday by a House committee show. An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that, despite receiving some licences, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and had not and would not ship to that firm. Century Litong says it has no dealings with Huang. Nvidia’s shares, meanwhile, have had their worst run since 2008.

This is the $500 scooter I'd choose as my daily driver on a budget

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For a lot of commuters who want an electric scooter to get to and from work, you don’t need a tricked-out ride that costs over $1,000 and keeps up with the Porsches on the road. Something much more modest — and affordable will do the trick.

I’ve recently been testing two scooters — the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go — which are made for commuters, and can be purchased for less than $600. I’ve found them to be fairly evenly matched, so to help you decide which is best for your needs, I’ve broken things down into a round-by-round comparison.

The Apollo Dash has a top speed of 22 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, and has a 600W motor and 480Wh battery.

The Segway E3 Go has a top speed of 20 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, a 400W motor, and front suspension.

The Apollo Dash is regularly priced at $699, but as of this writing, is on sale for $529 at Apollo.com; the Segway E3 Go is regularly $649, but for Black Friday, I've seen it on sale for $449.

Both of these scooters cut a pretty sleek profile. I personally like the cleaner lines of the Apollo as it transitions from the downtube to the deck; Segway’s folding mechanism, as well as its front suspension, makes things look a little busier

However, from a comfort standpoint, I liked the raked handlebars of the Segway over the Apollo, and the fact that the turn signal switch is located by your left thumb. By comparison, the Dash requires you to use your right thumb to activate the right turn signal, which means you have to take your thumb off the throttle.

The display is one area where Segway and Apollo really differ; the E3 Go has a more traditional color LCD screen that shows your speed and battery life. The Dash, on the other hand, uses a grid of white LEDs, which also shows your speed and battery life in a more basic way. However, The Apollo Dash also has a quad lock mount just below, so if you have a compatible phone case, you can use your phone as a digital dashboard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I like the folding mechanism on both scooters; you can collapse them in mere seconds, but I'm giving the advantage here to Segway. You can simply press on a flap with your foot, so you don't have to lean down.

Apollo’s scooter is slightly lighter than Segway’s — 43 pounds as opposed to 46.7 pounds. You’re going to get a workout either way.

One of my biggest concerns as a rider is being seen by other drivers. The Apollo’s large light bar, which extends the length of the downtube, makes you far more noticeable at night. In addition, you can adjust the angle of its headlight. By comparison, the Segway’s headlight is fixed, and it has no other lights in the front.

Both scooters have turn signals in the handlebars; however, only Apollo lets you adjust how long they remain on; from within the app, you can set a period from seven seconds or until you deactivate it.

I still wish both had turn signals in the rear of the scooter too, like the Segway Max G3 Plus or the Apollo City.

On my steep hill test (which has a max grade of 10%), the Segway slowed down to 4 MPH on the steepest section; I had to do a little wiggling of the handlebars to keep it balanced. By comparison, the Apollo managed to get up the same hill at 8 MPH — not exactly a speed record, but it was twice as fast as the Segway.

On a hill with a less steep grade of 5.7%, both scooters performed about the same, slowing to around 12 MPH.

The raked handlebars, front suspension, and larger tires of the Segway E3 Go really made a difference, especially at speed. The scooter felt more stable when I was cruising at 20+ MPH, and was much less jarring than the suspension-less Apollo when I went over bumps and potholes.

Both the Apollo and Segway are rated for a max distance of 25 miles, but that’s assuming ideal conditions, and if you poke along at around 9 MPH on a flat road. With both scooters at full charge, Segway estimated that it had 11.2 miles of range, compared to 17 for the Apollo when both were set to their max performance levels. If you want to eke out a bit more range, both scooters offer regenerative braking.

I took them one at a time on an identical 5.5-mile loop around my town, going up and down the same hills. After a 5.5-mile ride, the Apollo had 55% battery left, while Segway’s had just 32%.

Now, range will vary greatly from one rider to another, but I suspect that the more powerful motor in the Apollo scooter enabled it to use power more efficiently during my test.

Both Segway’s and Apollo’s apps let you customize how the scooter performs, to a certain extent. For example, with each, you can specify the max speed for each performance setting, so if you don’t want to zoom along at 20 MPH in Sport mode, you don’t have to.

However, Apollo’s app offers a bit more customization. You can, for instance, set the amount of time that the turn signals remain on, and also fine-tune the throttle response, if you want to get off to a faster start.

After testing both the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go, neither really pulls away from the other to make this a decisive victory. Still, over these seven rounds, the Apollo Dash takes this matchup, winning four rounds to the Segway E3 Go’s three.

I liked the design of the Segway’s handlebars and controls, and it felt more comfortable and stable while riding. And, at the time of this writing, it was $80 cheaper. However, the Apollo Dash proved more capable when scooting up hills, its lighting makes it far more visible, and it had a better range in my testing.

If you don't have hills to climb, then the Segway would be the better pick, but if you're facing some inclines, then I would lean towards the Apollo.

#3185. Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming in 2027

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the company will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a new round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will update the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too important – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

#3184. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

#3183. Microsoft Stock Gave Back 8% Within 2 Weeks of Its Record. Here's How Past Quick Pullbacks Like This Played Out.

Quick slides like this have hit the software giant 18 times since 1995. How many finished lower a year later?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 22, 2026 at 3:41AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›

Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) hit a record close of $555.80 on Nov. 4. Nine trading days later, on Nov. 17, it ended at $506.24 -- around 9% under the high. Shares trade near $508 as of this writing.

Part of that drop comes from the broader market. The Nasdaq-100 fell around 5% in the same stretch. But Microsoft fell more.

A fast drop from a new peak can feel like a warning. For Microsoft, it usually hasn't been one.

By my count of its daily closes, the stock has fallen this fast from a record on 18 past occasions since 1995. Shares were higher 12 months later in 15 of the cases, and the typical (median) gain was around 30%. That's about twice the median one-year gain of about 15% for all trading days in the same stretch.

Every case begins on the first day Microsoft closed at least 8% under a record close set within the past 15 trading days. I used split-adjusted closing prices without dividends and counted just one case per record, so a stock that kept falling couldn't count twice until it hit a new high.

"A year later" means the close 12 months after that first 8% day.

The recent record is especially strong. Since 2018, Microsoft has done this nine times, and the stock was higher a year later in all nine. The middle result was a rise of around 29%.

The best one came in September 2020, when shares rose about 48% over the next year.

But the ride was rarely smooth. Ten of the 18 saw shares fall at least another 10% before the year ended.

The latest case shows how rough that can be. Once the stock slid 8% under its Oct. 28, 2025, record, it eventually closed around 29% below where it stood on that 8% day. It didn't hit a new record until Oct. 13, 2026. And a year after the pullback started, it was up only about 7%.

The three cases that finished lower fell within around nine months of each other, in April 1999, July 1999, and January 2000. A year later, shares were down each time, by up to about 50%.

The last one was by far the worst. Microsoft set a record close on Dec. 27, 1999, and fell 8% under it in January 2000. It didn't close above its 1999 high again until October 2016 -- almost 17 years later.

One big difference between then and now is valuation. In all three cases, the stock cost more than 60 times the earnings Microsoft had reported in the previous four quarters.

Today, Microsoft's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings for its past four quarters are $18.04 per share, a number that leaves out the impact of its investments in OpenAI. The stock trades at around 28 times those earnings.

True, the stock arguably still has a premium price for a tech business this big. But it's nowhere near the multiples investors paid then.

Of course, earnings growth has cooled a little. Adjusted earnings per share climbed 18% year over year in Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the period ended Sept. 30, 2026). That was its slowest rate in at least four quarters, after growth between 21% and 24% in the previous three quarters.

What makes this case unusual is that Microsoft's Nov. 4 record came on a one-day jump of almost 7%. None of the 18 past records in this study came on a one-day gain larger than about 5%.

So a lot of the latest drop has just given that jump back. Measured from its Nov. 3 close of around $521, the stock is down only about 2%. In other words, the drop from the record likely overstates how much has changed for Microsoft since early November.

All in all, the record here looks promising for long-term shareholders. A quick 8% slide from a high has usually been followed by gains, and the exceptions were when the stock was priced well above where it is now.

But I don't see a reason to rush. More than half the time, buyers had a chance to pay at least 10% less at some point during the year.

And with earnings growth slowing and the stock still about 28 times adjusted earnings, I'd rather wait for a lower price than the one offered now.

If this pullback follows most of the others, that chance might come -- but history isn't a guarantee.

#3182. Anthropic researcher claims Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis

Levent Alpöge released the proof as computer-checked Lean code. Mathematicians say understanding it could take years.

Anthropic logo, Guilherand-Granges, France, March 2025

Mmathematician at Anthropic says he has used the company’s Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge made the claim in a note on his website on Friday, Bloomberg reported.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote.

The hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, concerns how prime numbers are spread out. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which carries a $1m prize. Alpöge says his proof also covers a broader version, the generalised Riemann hypothesis.

He did not publish a traditional paper. Instead, he released the proof in Lean, a programming language that checks every logical step. The code runs to about 17 million lines, Science reported.

Andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at MIT, told Bloomberg he had checked the code on his own computer. He said he had seen at least three other checks by professional mathematicians. Later on Friday, Sutherland put the chance that anything is wrong at roughly zero, Scientific American reported.

However, other mathematicians urged caution. A proof that compiles in Lean still has to state the right problem, and humans have to confirm that it does.

Kevin Buzzard, a professor at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof shows, Al Jazeera reported. The proof has not been formally accepted.

“This time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” he wrote.

Anthropic declined to comment to Bloomberg. The claim came a day after the company’s record stock market debut.

If confirmed, it would be the second Millennium Prize Problem that AI may have helped solve. In September, OpenAI said its models had produced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem.

5 films that prove why the Juilliard-trained actor is cut from the same cloth as De Niro and Pacino

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When I think about Adam Driver as an actor, two words come to mind: stoic and intense. I see a disciplined actor with no social media presence who lets his work speak for itself.

Part of that discipline comes from his military background, while the rest stems from his time at Juilliard. Driver would have loved to come up in the 1960s and 1970s, as he feels cut from the same cloth as Robert De Niro and Al Pacino.

Currently, Driver stars in “Paper Tiger,” James Gray’s New York City crime drama about two brothers whose business dealings become entangled with the Russian mob. Driver has received rave reviews for his performance, with some critics calling it the actor’s best work. In honor of “Paper Tiger,” here are Driver's five best movies.

The irony of Driver’s career is that despite being known for his intensity, he’s extremely funny. Driver’s breakout role came as Adam Sackler in the HBO comedy “Girls.” Since this list concerns movies, I’ll select another project from that era: “What If,” or in some territories, “The F Word.” (“What If” is a better title, for what it’s worth.) One night, Wallace (Daniel Radcliffe) and Chantry (Zoe Kazan) meet and hit it off. Although Chantry has a boyfriend, Wallace elects to be her friend because he’s in love with her.

Wallace and Chantry seem perfect for each other, but bad timing and unfortunate circumstances keep them apart. Driver plays Allan, Wallace’s best friend. Allan is a boisterous friend who encourages Wallace to tell Chantry how he feels. “What If” is a charming rom-com with a hilarious performance from Driver, who deserves recognition for his line delivery in the “greatest moment of my life” speech.

Like many “Star Wars” fans, I have problems with the sequel trilogy. My biggest gripe is with “The Rise of Skywalker,” especially the entire Palpatine debacle. It’s difficult to tell the story of Driver’s career without a “Star Wars” movie, so I’ll go with “The Force Awakens,” the highly entertaining popcorn blockbuster that kicked off Lucasfilm’s Disney era. Thirty years after the events of “Return of the Jedi,” the galaxy faces a new Imperial threat: the First Order.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Resistance, led by General Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher), recruits a new set of rebels, including Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), Finn (John Boyega), and Rey (Daisy Ridley). Driver plays Kylo Ren, a ruthless warrior in the First Order out to find the location of Luke Skywalker. Driver’s intensity translates seamlessly to a villainous role. Kylo is Gen Z’s version of Darth Vader. Driver plays Ren as a brooding, sad boy with daddy issues. It’s a subversion of masculinity and an interesting addition to the “Star Wars” lineup of iconic villains.

Spike Lee said it best. While speaking with BBC Radio 1 for “BlacKkKlansman,” Lee described Driver as a “beast.” Lee went on to praise Driver’s range as an actor. No arguments here, Mr. Lee. In “BlacKkKlansman,” John David Washington stars as Ron Stallworth, the first Black detective in the Colorado Springs Police Department.

Looking to infiltrate the local Ku Klux Klan, Ron poses as a white supremacist over the phone. The Klan buys it and wants to meet Ron. Since he’s Black, Ron recruits his white Jewish co-worker, Flip Zimmerman (Driver), to pose as him. The ruse works, and the duo infiltrates the Ku Klux Klan to thwart its nefarious plans. “BlacKkKlansman” is a witty and sharp critique of racism and extremist political movements.

It’s also a film that eerily resembles events from the current day, which is scary in itself. Driver’s grounded presence is the perfect counterbalance to Washington’s excessive charisma. Driver earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor, the first of his career.

I enjoy Driver as a heel. He knows how to get under my skin as a villain. He did it in “Star Wars,” and he arguably did it better in “The Last Duel.” Ridley Scott’s period piece is based on the last trial by combat in medieval France. The movie is split into three parts, detailing the viewpoints of Jean de Carrouges (Matt Damon), Jacques le Gris (Driver), and Marguerite de Carrouges (Jodie Comer).

Marguerite accuses Jacques of rape while Jean is out of town. With no physical evidence, it becomes Marguerite’s word versus Jacques’s, with the latter vehemently denying the accusation. Believing he must defend his family's honor, Jean requests a duel to the death, which Jacques accepts.

Don’t let the box office failures turn you away from this excellent drama and Scott’s best movie this decade. It’s a shockingly violent movie, but also one that rewards patience. It’s not good vs. bad. Instead, it’s about morally complex characters, making for a far more interesting dilemma.

If I were having trouble in a relationship, “Marriage Story” might be at the bottom of the pile of films to watch. Noah Baumbach’s drama about a couple going through a divorce features some of the meanest, rawest, and most emotional scenes I’ve ever seen. At times, it punches you in the heart and makes you question everything you knew about love. At the center of the movie are Charlie (Driver) and Nicole Barber (Scarlett Johansson), a married couple.

Charlie, a theater director, and Nicole, an actress, agree to a divorce. Charlie remains in New York, while Nicole heads to Los Angeles with their son, Henry (Azhy Robertson). The couple begins divorce proceedings cordially, but when lawyers get involved, it becomes cutthroat. Some of these scenes between Charlie and Nicole, especially the climactic argument, are like watching a car crash — you can’t look away. It’s an acting tour de force for Driver and Johansson, who earned their respective Oscar nominations.

#3179. I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again

We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

#3178. Taiwan widens its short-selling ban after the Taiex’s worst week since 1991

The island’s NT$500bn stabilisation fund says it has been buying shares since 6 November as AI stocks slump.

Taiwan’s financial regulator has banned all short selling of local stocks below the previous day’s closing price. The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) announced the move on Saturday, Bloomberg reported. It takes effect on 23 November.

Short selling is a bet that a share price will fall. The ban covers both margin short sales and sales of borrowed shares. Securities and futures firms that short stocks to hedge their business are exempt.

The FSC also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130%. In addition, it stopped taking applications from brokers to list new put warrants, which also pay out when prices fall.

It is the third round of short-selling curbs this month. On 9 November, the FSC cut the cap on intraday short sales of borrowed shares from 30% to 3% of average daily volume, Crowdfund Insider reported.

A second round on 19 November banned shorting below the previous close for stocks that fell at least 3.5% the day before, according to Focus Taiwan.

Neither round stopped the slide. The Taiex fell 6.2% on Friday and lost almost 18% over the week, its worst week since 1991, according to Bloomberg. Doubts about whether AI spending will pay off have hit tech shares across Asia.

Meanwhile, Taiwan’s NT$500bn ($15bn) National Financial Stabilization Fund said it has been buying shares since 6 November. The fund said worries about tighter US regulation of AI, returns on big capital spending and margin-financing risks had triggered the sell-off.

Taiwan’s finance ministry said the economy remains strong. It grew 14.4% in the third quarter, and October export orders rose 78% from a year earlier, Bloomberg reported.

#3177. Is This Cryptocurrency a Potential Millionaire Maker?

Hyperliquid has been skyrocketing in value, but does it have the long-term staying power required to mint new millionaires?

By Dominic Basulto – Nov 22, 2026 at 4:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Hyperliquid ›

One of the few bright spots in the crypto market has been Hyperliquid (HYPE +1.89%), up 140% for the year. Since its launch in late 2024, the HYPE token is up a remarkable 1,800%.

But can Hyperliquid hold on to these gains and surge even higher in the years ahead? If so, it could be a millionaire maker. But before you start shopping for luxury yachts and high-end vacation homes, here's what you need to know about Hyperliquid.

First and foremost, Hyperliquid still faces tremendous regulatory obstacles. That's because Hyperliquid is a decentralized crypto exchange based offshore, and it doesn't yet have regulatory permission to operate in the U.S. or to offer its services to U.S. retail investors. If you try to trade on the Hyperliquid platform, you will immediately get a red warning message that you're in a restricted jurisdiction.

Granted, President Donald Trump has given regulators the green light to bring Hyperliquid to the U.S. That's a huge positive. But the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) recently warned that Hyperliquid would be treated just like any other entity. Until it receives formal regulatory approval, Hyperliquid will need to partner with a registered exchange to offer financial derivatives to U.S. retail investors.

Meanwhile, the number of participants lining up to offer perpetual futures -- the financial product that led to Hyperliquid's meteoric rise -- seems to increase by the day. That's because the CFTC gave the go-ahead for crypto perps in May and for equity perps in November, which has dramatically changed the competitive landscape.

It's not just decentralized exchanges such as Hyperliquid that are potential rivals. Centralized crypto exchanges such as Coinbase Global (COIN -6.34%) and trading platforms like Robinhood Markets (HOOD -9.44%) are also potential rivals. So are prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket. And what if legacy Wall Street financial exchanges decide to get into the act?

You get the idea. Competition could be off the charts, and that means Hyperliquid may start to account for a shrinking share of trading in perpetual futures. If that's the case, there's no way that it can grow at triple-digit percentage rates in coming years.

And here's the really scary fact: Hyperliquid is now down 37% from its all-time high of $97.98 in September. If roughly $100 were the top for HYPE, it wouldn't surprise me at all. In the crypto market, it's normal for highly volatile cryptos to skyrocket in price one year, only to collapse the next.

All of this is to say: Don't believe the hype about HYPE.

Given that almost all cryptocurrencies are down this year, it's easy to suspend disbelief and think that Hyperliquid might be a magic ticket to millionaire status. But I just don't think it has the staying power required to mint new millionaires. Hyperliquid might be beating the pants off Bitcoin (BTC +0.30%) this year, but I'd still rather buy Bitcoin.

Thankfully, entry-level luxury crossovers exist, and they’re some of the smartest buys on the market. For my next comparison, I’m pitting the Mini Countryman and Audi Q3 against each other in a head-to-head matchup to see which compact crossover is worth buying.

Each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory. It’s actually been years since I last tested a Mini — the electric Countryman EV — so you can imagine how eager I was to get back into the gas-powered 2027 Mini Countryman S All4.

With an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin. I will say, however, that you can’t dismiss the Q3 just yet, because after a week’s worth of driving, it too impressed me on plenty of occasions.

2.0-Liter MINI TwinPower Turbo Inline 4-Cylinder Engine

22 mpg city / 29 mpg highway / 25 mpg combined

24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway / 27 mpg combined

Frankly, this one’s tough because these compact crossovers cater to completely different tastes, so personal preference heavily influences the decision.

The 2026 Audi Q3 leans heavily into conventional luxury aesthetics, dressed in Malpelo Blue Metallic with the Black Optic package — which shimmers in the light. Alongside the sharp LED headlights up front and OLED taillights in the back, the package makes it look sleek and unmistakably upscale.

By contrast, the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 embraces a sportier edge and distinctive British flair. It’s undeniably boxier and more upright, yet it’s loaded with personality — I especially love its Slate Blue Metallic paint job with a contrasting black roof and stripes. Even its LED lighting features customizable light signatures to match its charming looks.

Ultimately, it comes down to whether you prefer understated German luxury or retro-modern charm — making this category an easy tie.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Looking at their spec sheets, it’s quite clear that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 holds a slight advantage in terms of fuel economy with an EPA-estimated 27 mpg combined (24 city / 32 highway), compared to the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro’s 25 mpg combined rating (22 city / 29 highway).

In my real-world testing, however, that gap turned into a surprisingly wide canyon. Over 313.6 miles of mixed driving in the Countryman, I averaged an impressive 31.1 mpg overall — easily exceeding its EPA estimate. Better yet, it hit 30.5 mpg on my best short-distance trip and soared to 36.1 mpg on a longer highway stretch.

In contrast, the Audi Q3 struggled to match its window sticker across 243.5 miles of testing, averaging just 23.2 mpg overall. Even on my best long-distance (26.5 mpg) run, it never came close to its 29 mpg highway rating.

If keeping fuel costs low is a top priority, the Mini is the clear standout here, saving you noticeably more at the pump in the long run.

Most compact crossovers prioritize fuel economy and put driving dynamics in the back seat, but not these two. Better yet, I love how both prove you don’t need a massive engine to have fun behind the wheel.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 is my favorite of the two by a narrow margin, packing a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four engine that puts out 241 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque. The Audi similarly has impressive muscle under the hood: a 2.0-liter TFSI four-cylinder that delivers 255 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque.

What I will say after being behind the wheel of both is that they’re noticeably zippy off the line, with speedy acceleration that makes it effortless to overtake at cruising speed. While the Q3’s powertrain actually surprised me with a smooth delivery that almost makes it feel more like an EV, it doesn’t beat the Countryman when the road starts to curve. The Mini's lower, wider stance keeps it feeling noticeably more planted through corners, preserving that signature go-kart agility it’s known for.

Despite their smaller footprints, these compact crossovers still offer plenty of room to make lengthy road trips a breeze. However, the 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 holds a slight advantage. That’s because it offers 40.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches in the rear, which beats the 2026 Audi Q3’s 40 inches up front and 36.1 inches in the back. Additionally, they deliver nearly identical trunk space around 25 cubic feet, easily accommodating my electric scooter.

Inside, they take very different approaches to cabin materials. The Audi leans into traditional luxury with genuine leather seating surfaces, wood inlays, and solid soundproofing that keeps road noise at a minimum. Obviously, the higher price of the Q3 is justified by its more luxurious aesthetics.

Mini takes a totally different approach that gives it a charming style that feels genuinely original. It trades classic leather for Vescin leather-free upholstery and knitted textile surfaces on the dash and doors — which I have to say looked funky and stylish at first glance, but they eventually grew on me.

Sure, the Audi comes up a smidge short on rear legroom, but the Q3 just feels noticeably more plush over long stretches. And when I factor in Audi’s smoother, more intuitive adaptive cruise assist on highways, the Q3 edges ahead as the more relaxing cruiser.

Audi needs to prove it’s worth spending about $7,500 more over its rival. But does it?

While the 2026 Audi Q3 doesn’t skimp on luxury amenities, it simply makes you pay noticeably more for them. Even so, I appreciate its crisp 360-degree camera coverage, head-up display that projects driving details onto the windshield to lessen distractions, and seamless Park Assist Plus for automatic parking. Inside, its panoramic sunroof and vibrant LED ambient lighting create a more upscale look at night — while its large blind-spot warning lights mounted right on the side mirrors are impossible to miss in heavy traffic or in the daytime.

However, you’re still getting better value for the money out of the Mini Countryman S ALL4. For starters, its circular 9.4-inch OLED touchscreen display is a sight to behold and runs a far more intuitive interface. Although it ditches the traditional driver’s cluster entirely, the flip-up head-up display keeps distractions at a minimum. I’m also big on sound, and the punchy Harman Kardon surround sound system easily outclasses the Audi's Sonos setup.

Not only does it offer full 360-degree camera coverage, but it also includes a clever Backup Assistant that takes over the wheel and automatically retraces the path I took to get into the spot. And finally, I really love the adaptive LED headlights with customizable light signatures and cornering lights.

When I weigh this robust feature set against that $7,540 price gap, the Mini delivers far more bang for your buck.

Let me finish by saying that I’d gladly buy either compact crossover in a heartbeat with my own money. That said, the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro does come up short once the tallies are counted.

If you prioritize traditional luxury materials, a quieter cabin, and a smoother adaptive cruise control system for long highway commutes, it remains an immensely likable daily driver that costs less than the average luxury vehicle. Honestly, despite losing this head-to-head matchup, I would still gladly buy the Audi Q3 — it’s just that the Mini Countryman gives you more for less.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 emerges as the clear winner, and it’s the one I’d ultimately pick. Between its punchy driving dynamics, standout real-world fuel economy, sharper OLED infotainment system, and $7,540 price advantage in this comparison, it simply delivers too much personality and value to ignore.
