#3088. 3 Reasons to Claim Social Security at 70

It's one of the best ways to maximize lifetime benefits.

By Stefon Walters – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:13AM EST

For most American retirees, Social Security plays a large role in their retirement income. In some cases, it's most of their income; in many, it's all of their retirement income. That's why the decision of when to claim shouldn't be glossed over.

You can begin claiming benefits at age 62, but your benefit will be reduced, making it a trade-off some aren't willing to take. You can also delay benefits until age 70, which has the opposite effect, but is it worth it?

Your full retirement age is when you're qualified to receive your full monthly benefit, called your primary insurance amount (PIA). For anyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is currently 67, but you can delay benefits until you turn 70 and receive a bump for each month you delay past 67.

For each month you delay benefits past your full retirement age, you'll receive Delayed Retirement Credits (DRCs) equal to two-thirds of 1% monthly. This works out to 8% annually, and a 24% total boost if your full retirement age is 67 and you delay until 70.

In many cases, waiting for the increased monthly benefits results in a higher lifetime payout.

Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is added as a percentage to someone's current benefits. By delaying benefits until 70 and securing a higher monthly benefit, you also lock in larger dollar raises with each COLA.

For example, if your PIA is $2,000, next year's 3.6% COLA would raise it to $2,072. However, if you delayed benefits until 70, boosting your benefit to $2,480, a 3.6% COLA would raise it to $2,569.

That's an extra $204 for the year just from the one COLA, but over time, the larger dollar increases compound.

Social Security survivor benefits provide benefit support for a surviving spouse after the primary earner passes away.

Unlike spousal benefits -- which allow the claiming spouse to receive up to 50% of the primary spouse's PIA -- the person receiving survivor benefits receives 100% of the dead spouse's benefit, including any DRCs received.

As an example, let's return to someone whose PIA is $2,000, meaning they'd receive $2,480 if they delayed benefits until age 70. If their spouse claims spousal benefits, they could receive up to $1,000 in benefits, even though the primary spouse is receiving more than their PIA. However, if the primary spouse passes away, the surviving spouse could receive the full $2,480.

#3086. 3 Retirement Expenses You May Not Be Prepared For -- But Need to Be

Don't let these costs catch you off guard.

By Maurie Backman – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:18AM EST

Retirement is often portrayed as a time when you finally get to enjoy the money you've spent decades saving. You may have plans to travel, spend more time with family, pursue hobbies, or simply enjoy a slower pace of life.

But the expenses you don't see coming could easily derail your retirement plans and deplete your savings sooner than expected. Here are three big retirement expenses you need to prepare for in advance so you aren't thrown for a loop.

Many people are able to pay off their mortgages ahead of retirement. But don't assume that your housing costs will be negligible just because you're mortgage-free. Your home will continue to require maintenance. And as it ages, you might need to sink more money into repairs that can be surprisingly expensive.

There's also the possibility that you may eventually need to modify your home to make it safer and more accessible as you age. Installing grab bars, adding better lighting, or creating wider doorways to accommodate a walker could all require additional spending.

To avoid a shock, maintain a cash emergency fund outside of your IRA or 401(k), which may be more heavily invested in stocks and other assets whose value can fluctuate. Home repairs in particular are often things that can't wait, so having cash on hand to cover them is key. You may also want to maintain a separate account for eventual renovations if your goal is to age in place.

Once you retire, you may have more time to spend money on hobbies, travel, dining out, and social activities. Some of these expenses, like new subscriptions, might seem relatively small individually, but they can add up over time. And if you want to travel a lot, that's something your budget will need to accommodate.

It's important to create a realistic entertainment budget that reflects the retirement lifestyle you actually want. If you're looking to go overseas three times a year, work that into your financial plan instead of winging it on the spot.

You may also want to take some strategic steps to make your desired lifestyle possible. Working an extra year or two to boost savings could help, as could delaying your Social Security benefits for larger monthly checks.

You might assume that Medicare will cover most of your healthcare needs as you get older. But Medicare generally doesn't cover ongoing custodial care, such as assistance with bathing, dressing, eating, and other everyday activities. That means you could be responsible for a substantial portion of the cost, if not all of it, if you eventually need in-home assistance, assisted living, or nursing home care.

The latest CareScout 2025 Cost of Care Survey highlights just how expensive these services have become. Here are the median costs of various types of care on a national level:

Because these figures represent national medians, it's important to recognize that costs in your area could be considerably higher. So don't wait until you need long-term care to start thinking about how you'll pay for it.

Research long-term-care insurance, hybrid life insurance policies with long-term-care benefits, and other potential funding options. Also think about what type of care you'd prefer as you get older and whether your retirement savings can support those expenses.

Ultimately, retirement planning isn't just about having enough money to stop working. It's about having enough money to handle the unexpected while still enjoying the lifestyle you've worked so hard to achieve. Preparing for these three expenses in advance could help prevent unwanted financial stress later.

#3085. What to Buy (and Skip) on Black Friday 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Electronics, small appliances, toys and clothes make the list, along with some out-of-the-box buys.

Black Friday comes but once a year — although sometimes it feels like it lasts for a month. The big day is Nov. 27, but the sales have already started.

If you’ve been sitting on a holiday shopping list and waiting for prices to drop, we’ve got good news: It’s time to start your shopping engines! (So to speak.)

You don’t need a calendar full of sale dates to navigate the shopping frenzy. Focus on the categories likely to offer the biggest savings. Here’s what to buy, and what can wait.

If you’ve got top-priority toys on your list, buy them at a discount if you can find them, says Kristin McGrath, senior editor at The Krazy Coupon Lady, “just in case they don’t go down in price later.”

Non-electronic toys are a good bet, says Julie Ramhold, consumer analyst with DealNews.com, because they’re less affected by tariffs on electronic components. That includes Legos, dolls and playsets.

NeeDoh squishies are a hot stocking stuffer this year and may be in short supply. At authorized retailers like Target, they should be relatively affordable, but try to avoid unauthorized resellers who may crank up the price, Ramhold says.

While you may see mattress stores offering a few doorbusters on Black Friday, don’t feel pressured to jump on a deal.

“Mattresses tend to see some of their strongest discounts around major sales events like Labor Day and Presidents Day,” says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, shopping and savings strategist with Rakuten. “So if you’re not in a rush, it may be worth waiting for one of those windows.”

Similarly, bedding and towels are often on deep discount during January white sales, Feinstein Gerstley says.

Got some counter space and an itch for a new food processor? Black Friday sales are a great time to price surf for countertop appliances, including blenders, juicers and air fryers.

“Those things we see sometimes half off or more,” McGrath says. “And they’re all on sale at the same time, so any one you’re looking for is likely to have a discount.”

Holiday decor is only a must-buy during Black Friday sales if you need it for this holiday season.

While you’ll still see sales on holiday items like artificial trees, drinkware and garlands, “if you can wait until after Christmas, that’s when discounts should reach up to 80% or more at stores like Target, Walmart and department stores like JCPenney and Macy’s,” Ramhold says.

Electronics are typically a slam-dunk buy at this time of year. “Every store is competing for your business, so televisions, headphones, tablets, laptops — they’re all going to be on sale at the same time,” McGrath says.

Gaming consoles, in particular, see some of the better discounts. And they often come bundled with a gift card, gaming accessories or video games. “Consoles are common gifts,” McGrath says. “The stores know that, so they’re offering competitive deals.”

That said, the traditional deep discounts you usually see on electronics for Black Friday may be a little lackluster this year due to high prices on parts, Ramhold says.

For best results, research the exact specs of the product you want and put it in your cart ahead of time, says consumer savings expert Andrea Woroch. That way, if a similar (but not identical) product goes on sale, you won’t accidentally buy the wrong thing.

You’ll usually find deeper discounts on items that are associated with fitness resolutions after New Year’s Day.

“Big-box retailers like Target and department stores like Macy’s will offer up to 40% off or more on both fitness equipment and activewear during early January sales,” Ramhold says.

Many fashion retailers offer Black Friday sales, McGrath says. So if there’s an item you stock in multiple colors or a work staple you need to replace, keep an eye on your favorite sites for the markdowns.

Shoes, too, are a category to eyeball, including seasonal buys and everyday options like running shoes, Ramhold says. “Some retailers may offer a BOGO promotion of some kind, but it’ll likely just be a ‘buy one, get one for 50% off,’” she says.

Just shop early for your size and color before inventory runs low, McGrath says. “You don’t want to miss out if there's a great deal.”

One caveat: Winter apparel will usually see bigger discounts toward the end of the year, Woroch says. So wait on your boot and coat purchases if you can.

Black Friday also offers the chance to snag deals on things you can use throughout the year:

Photo gifts: Whether you’re ordering holiday cards or putting together a photo book for your in-laws (or yourself), you can usually find sales from vendors like Snapfish and Shutterfly, among others.

Fitness classes: Try your local gym, yoga or Pilates studio for discounts on class packs. “I’ll buy a 20-class package, and it’s always a great deal,” Woroch says.

Spa services: Check local businesses for deals on massages, manicures and other self-care treatments.

Streaming subscriptions: If you’re a new customer (or canceled at least a month ago), some streaming platforms offer deep Black Friday discounts.

Black Friday deals are as much about strategy as savings, so make sure you’re maximizing your spending with these tips:

Let AI help. Tools like ChatGPT and Gemini can do a lot of the legwork for you. Write out a product name and try prompts like “Find the lowest price for X product by comparing every retail site that it’s sold on and including coupons and cash back offers,” Woroch says. (Just note that AI searches can be limited and may not find every deal available.)

Check the price, not just the percentage: “Sometimes the base price is inflated or it was listed initially for a higher price,” Feinstein Gerstley says. “Another retailer might have the same item for less, even if their discount doesn't look as impressive.”

Use a browser extension or cash-back app. As long as you’re spending money, recapture some of it with a browser extension or cash-back app that sends a percentage of your purchase back to you.

#3083. The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 5th Time This Century, and History Says It's Obvious What Comes Next for Stocks

If things seem too perfect for investors, they often are.

By Sean Williams – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:36AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

With less than six weeks left in 2026, investors have little to complain about. The mature-stock-driven Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -1.93%), broad-based S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%), and tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) have all catapulted to several record highs this year, driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, better-than-expected corporate earnings, and initial public offering euphoria.

While Wall Street's major stock indexes have made a habit of climbing the proverbial wall of worry and rising over the long term, history also makes clear that bull markets don't last forever. If things seem too perfect for investors, they often are.

Though any number of headwinds can knock the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite off their respective pedestals, one stands out. We're currently witnessing the stock market do something for only the fifth time this century, and history doesn't mince its words about what comes next for stocks.

Despite a parabolic move in outstanding margin debt sending all the wrong signals, the biggest worry for Wall Street and investors is premium stock valuations.

To be clear, past events can't guarantee what the future holds. Nevertheless, history has shown a tendency to rhyme on Wall Street more often than not, making it an excellent teaching tool for those investors willing to listen.

Most investors rely on the time-tested price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio when evaluating individual companies or the broader market. While the P/E ratio, which is derived using trailing 12-month earnings per share (EPS), is incredibly useful for quickly sizing up mature businesses, it can lose its utility entirely when recessions occur and EPS turns negative.

For Wall Street's broad-market stock indexes, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio (CAPE Ratio), is a far superior valuation tool. The Shiller P/E is based on average inflation-adjusted EPS over the trailing 10 years, meaning recessions won't render it useless.

Though economists introduced the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio less than four decades ago, it's been backtested to January 1871. Over these 156 years, the average reading is a relatively modest 17.45. As of the closing bell on Nov. 17, it was 38.76, or 122% above this long-term average.

Stock Market Shiller PE Ratio on the verge of taking out its Dot Com Bubble all-time high 🚨 🤯 👀 https://t.co/CtCmSgWnLt

What's particularly interesting is how the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have behaved once the CAPE Ratio surpasses 30, which has happened six times since January 1871, and five times this century, including the present:

On the one hand, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E can't pinpoint when the major stock indexes will peak or which catalyst(s) will send stocks tumbling. But this arbitrary line in the sand has an impeccable track record of foreshadowing significant downturns (20% or greater) in the stock market's major indexes.

History makes it crystal clear that premium valuations aren't sustainable on Wall Street.

Sometimes, history doesn't offer the most glowing forecast for the stock market. But altering your perspective can vastly change the projected outcome.

To state what can be an unpleasant truth, stock market corrections, bear markets, and even occasional crashes are normal and healthy events. Given that most of these events are driven by investor emotions, there's not much that can be done from a fiscal or monetary policy perspective to prevent them. Consider these events the cost of admission to take part in one of the world's greatest wealth creators.

But stock market corrections, bear markets, and crashes share an important trait: they're historically short-lived.

The analysts at Bespoke Investment Group examined every S&P 500 bull and bear market since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929, finding a sizable gap between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.

According to Bespoke's data set, released in late May, the average S&P 500 bear market finds its trough in 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months), while the typical bull market persists for 1,023 calendar days, or nearly 3.6 times as long.

The analysts at Crestmont Research took things even further by examining the rolling 20-year total returns of the benchmark S&P 500 since 1900. Since the S&P wasn't incepted until 1923, this meant tracking the total return of its components in other major indexes back to 1900.

Crestmont's data yielded 107 separate rolling 20-year periods (1900-1919, 1901-1920, and so on, through 2006-2025), all of which generated a positive average annual return.

Hypothetically speaking, since S&P 500-tracking funds didn't exist on U.S. exchanges until January 1993, if an investor had purchased an S&P 500 index fund at any point between 1900 and 2006 and simply held it for 20 years, they would have generated a profit every single time, including dividends. It didn't matter if they bought near a top, before a recession, depression, war, pandemic, or high inflation... the result was always the same.

Even when the stock market gives investors lemons, history says make some lemonade and be patient.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates rose enough today that you might be feeling some sticker shock.

If you're here looking for lower mortgage interest rates, today is definitely not your day.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.38% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points higher than yesterday and 12 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Keep in mind that mortgage rates are always on the move, and that if you're tracking rates day-to-day, you're going to see a lot of volatility. Zooming out and looking at the bigger picture — like a graph showing at least a month's worth of rate data — can help you see the overall trend.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.88% or higher — but there aren’t many people for whom that’s true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›

Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%) has long been a poster child for dividend stocks and a great source of income for many investors. On Dec. 15, it will pay the final $0.53 per share quarterly payment of its $2.12 annual commitment for this year. Using $2.12 as the benchmark, it would take 4,717 shares to achieve a $10,000 annual dividend payout.

Coca-Cola likely won't announce next year's dividend until sometime in February, but if we assume it increases to $2.20 per share (in line with recent increases), you would need 4,546 shares.

At the time of writing, Coca-Cola's stock was $98, so it would take $462,266 or $445,508 invested to instantly put you in position to earn $10,000 annually. Realistically, that's not possible for the vast majority of investors -- it takes time to build a stake. Luckily, if there's a dividend stock you can trust over the long haul, it's Coca-Cola.

With 64 consecutive years of dividend increases, it's in the exclusive Dividend Kings club (companies with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend increases). Coca-Cola has a stronghold in the non-alcoholic beverage industry (and a growing alcoholic beverage portfolio), brand recognition and loyalty that's second to none, global distribution, and healthy finances, so I don't see that streak stopping anytime soon (if ever).

Coca-Cola's stock is up close to 40% this year (as of Nov. 19), so its yield isn't as high as it typically is, but it's a good blue chip dividend stock to buy and hold.

#3080. Asked on Reddit: I Lost My Job; What Should I Do First?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Income loss is stressful; the first steps involve cutting costs and focusing on essentials.

A Redditor recently shared that they were struggling to decide which financial steps to take first after a job loss.

Should they withdraw money from retirement savings to have more cash on hand — but pay an early withdrawal penalty? Or is it better to rely on the severance payout to handle expenses?

Many users responded with good ideas: File for unemployment, try to avoid tapping into retirement savings, and cut expenses as much as possible.

For more ideas, I asked three financial experts how to manage money in the immediate aftermath of job loss.

While it’s tempting to make quick decisions about tapping into a retirement fund or selling a house, it’s better to wait on any big moves, says Parker Wine, retirement planning advisor at the financial firm Daniel A. White & Associates in Lewes, Delaware.

That’s because you need time to digest the situation and weigh the pros and cons of different options, he says. “People can get impulsive and panic, and it’s usually a bad thing to make decisions when you’re panicking,” he says.

Take your time, get second opinions and think through all of your options first, Wine suggests.

If you’re fortunate enough to receive a severance package, wait to sign it until you’ve reviewed it carefully and understand all of the details, says John Rafferty, partner and investment advisor representative at Solomon Financial in Carmel, Indiana.

For example, make sure you know about your health insurance options, such as whether you’ll receive insurance through COBRA or need to take out a new policy in the health insurance marketplace.

Filing for unemployment and checking into any other available workplace benefits — such as help with your new job search — is also an important part of understanding what support to expect in the weeks and months ahead, Rafferty adds.

Creating a bare-bones budget stripped of “extras” like restaurant meals or travel can help the severance payment last as long as possible, Rafferty says.

“Now that you don’t have income coming in, ask yourself, ‘How much can I spend and where?’”

You might be able to cut back on entertainment costs, coffee runs and clothing purchases, for example.

At the same time, it’s important to prioritize the essentials like mortgage payments, rent, utilities and food. Rafferty recommends calling your mortgage company, utilities provider and any other lenders to ask if they have a hardship program for those experiencing financial challenges.

Opting in could give you more time to pay your bills or temporarily lower payments.

It’s hard to stick to a budget that eliminates all entertainment, so Rafferty suggests finding enjoyable activities that come with a low price tag. Hiking, discovering a new park and participating in free community events are all ways to enjoy downtime on a budget.

“Having that release is mentally a big thing so you can stay prepared for the job search,” he says. “Otherwise, it’s easy to get down and feel negative, and we need things to help us feel positive.”

Similarly, connecting with friends and family during this time is crucial, says Laura Adams, accredited financial counselor and financial coach in Wilmington, North Carolina.

People often feel a sense of shame or embarrassment after job loss, and Adams encourages people to talk about their feelings and ask for help if needed. “Financial shame can cause us to make emotional rather than confident financial decisions,” she says.

Starting some kind of side hustle to bring in extra cash can also help bridge the gap between the job loss and your next job, Wine says. Substitute teaching, working at a local public golf course and driving for a rideshare service are all options he’s seen people try.

Doing something new also helps stave off boredom while unemployed, but he cautions that you’ll still owe taxes on any side income you bring in, so plan accordingly.

All three financial experts also emphasized that a job loss is easier to handle with an emergency savings fund you can turn to, and suggested building one up — ideally three to six months’ worth of expenses. But starting small helps, too — while employed, if possible.

The Redditor who posted the question mentioned that, like many Americans, they lacked emergency savings. This added urgency to the question of what to prioritize.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like how to deal with job loss, so we sifted through Reddit forums to get a pulse check. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

#3079. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

#3078. Home Depot Just Delivered Great News to Investors

Home Depot reported its best same-store sales growth in years.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:05AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Home Depot ›

Home Depot (HD +0.70%) delivered investors great news when it reported its strongest same-store sales growth since the third quarter of 2022, which largely came under the watchful eye of CFO Richard McPhail while CEO Ted Decker was on medical leave. McPhail will now take the helm of the company coming off one of its strongest quarters in years, while Decker will become chairman.

McPhail said the company won't change course under his leadership, which makes sense. Over the past several years, Home Depot has been putting more emphasis on professional customers. McPhail has played a big role in that, helping oversee the recent acquisitions of SRS Distribution in 2024 and GMS last fall. Ann-Marie Campbell, who ran the day-to-day operations while Decker was out, will become chief operating officer.

The executive moves remove some uncertainty around Decker's health and put a team in charge that just helped Home Depot report its best quarterly results in years. While the stock didn't have a strong reaction, these changes should serve the home improvement company well going forward.

The home improvement environment has been very tough the past four years. COVID stay-at-home restrictions pulled forward a lot of big home renovation projects, while rising interest rates have affected both housing turnover and financing. It was great to see Home Depot turn in 2.2% comparable-store growth both globally and in the U.S. It was also the sixth straight quarter that both have been positive, showing the strides the company has been making.

Below is a table of the improvements the company has been seeing in its same-store sales growth.

Source: Home Depot earnings reports. Home Depot's fiscal quarters end approximately one month after standard calendar quarters. Table by author.

The same-store sales growth was fueled by a 3% increase in average ticket size, as the number of transactions sank by 0.5%. Higher-ticket items drove the growth, with same-store sales on transactions over $1,000 climbing 4.5%, led by strength in power and appliances.

Management called out strength in power, which saw double-digit comp growth. Storage, plumbing, and electrical all saw mid-single-digit growth. Overall, 13 of Home Depot's 16 product categories recorded positive same-store sales growth. Both pros and DIY (do-it-yourself) turned in positive same-store sales, with Pro outperforming. Digital sales, meanwhile, jumped 13%.

Home Depot's total revenue increased 4.9% year over year to $43.4 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) rose 3% to $3.86. These results topped the analyst consensus calling for adjusted EPS of $3.84 on $42.8 billion in sales, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Looking ahead, Home Depot updated its full-year guidance for sales to grow 4.5% with a 1.4% increase in same-store sales and a 2% increase in adjusted EPS. It will open 15 new stores this year. The company previously guided for same-store sales growth of flat to up 2% and total sales growth of 2.5% to 4.5%, with adjusted EPS growth of flat to up 4%.

Home Depot looks like it has turned the corner with another quarter of positive same-store sales growth. However, the current environment likely won't get easier. That's why its focus on professional customers, which continue to outperform, should remain its main focus.

The latest Leading Indicator of Remodeling Activity (LIRA) projections, which are published by the Joint Center for Housing Studies at Harvard University, show another likely slowdown next year. Given the state of the economy and higher rates compared to much of this past decade, that shouldn't be surprising.

Image source: https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/media/2026-10/lira_2026q3.png.

Source: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University.

Turning to valuation, Home Depot stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 21 times fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) analyst estimates. That's reasonable for a blue chip stock that has been weathering a difficult environment for several years. As such, I consider the stock a solid core type of holding.

#3076. Not Lucid. Not Ford. The EV Stock Most Likely to Catch Every Refunded Cybertruck Buyer.

With Tesla ending production of the Cybertruck, EV buyers have one clear destination.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:07AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Rivian Automotive ›

Tesla (TSLA -7.64%) is no stranger to controversy, at least partly thanks to its polarizing CEO Elon Musk. However, the company's products themselves can be just as "engaging" as its CEO, highlighted by the Cybertruck. Some people loved its looks; others thought it was ugly. Either way, Cybertruck production is ending. Here's why Rivian (RIVN -8.50%) could see a huge boost at just the right time as potential Cybertruck customers look elsewhere for an all-electric truck.

Elon Musk has stated that Tesla is dropping the Cybertruck so it can focus on producing Cybercabs. This may be true to some degree, but there have long been suspicions that the Cybertruck wasn't selling well. That may have changed after the electric vehicle maker announced plans to shut the production line in around eight months, which led to a flood of new orders.

That's not actually surprising, as the announcement likely brought forward demand. The cancellation of the Cybertruck could also have pushed people who like to own "exclusive" things, as well as those who like to flip products with limited supply, to jump in line. Regardless, it looks like there's now going to be more demand than supply. If customers still want an all-electric truck after the Cybertruck is no more, there's one vehicle maker that stands out: Rivian.

Rivian started out making all-electric high-end trucks and work trucks. The consumer vehicles it makes are stylish and have won multiple awards. However, the cost limited their appeal. This wasn't a tactical mistake; it was part of the plan. Like Tesla, Rivian started at the high end to maximize revenue per vehicle while it built out its business. The long-term goal was to expand production by bringing out a lower-cost, mass-market vehicle.

That vehicle, the R2, has just started to hit the market. It is already Rivian's best-selling model. Notably, the company's revenues rose 38% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, following the R2 launch, with deliveries up 46%. That success isn't surprising, given the R2 is a new, lower-cost model. The real key to Rivian's success is maintaining demand over the long term. Tesla's cancellation of the Cybertruck just increased the chances of that happening.

There are other options. For example, Lucid (LCID -10.39%) is working on an SUV, and Ford Motor Company (F -0.62%) has the iconic F-150. Neither of those fits quite as well as Rivian's R2. And that fact could be huge for Rivian and its shareholders.

Rivian has achieved significant success, building a company from the ground up that designs and manufactures all-electric trucks. However, it still isn't sustainably profitable. That's the real end goal. To get there, the company needs to increase volume so it can spread its costs across more vehicles. The R2 is intended to push the company in that direction.

It remains to be seen if the R2 can move the needle enough for Rivian to become profitable. The company has already produced a gross profit, meaning it generates more revenue from selling its products than it costs to produce them. Unfortunately, that gross profit has been supported by its software and services operations. And it still has to cover other costs, such as selling, general, and administrative expenses, as well as research and development spending, before it is in the black.

If the Cybertruck's cancellation leads to more R2 orders, it could be the extra push Rivian needs. More aggressive investors may want to take a second look at the stock now that Tesla is stepping away from the truck market.

Higher borrowing costs aren't the whole story. Here's what to consider before putting your house hunt on hold.

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

One bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how quickly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.)

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

#3074. Altria Yields 5.8% and Has Raised Its Dividend 61 Times in 57 Years. Here's Exactly How Much $5,000 Invested Pays Each Year.

Investors starting out with relatively small stakes can extract a fair amount of income from Altria.

By Todd Shriber – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:10AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Altria Group ›

One issue that new investors often grapple with is whether to buy stocks with small amounts of capital or wait until they have more substantial cash to enter the game.

Hint: Starting small is better than waiting or not starting at all. Some experts call it micro-investing, but whatever the label, prospective market participants, particularly those with the luxury of time on their side, are best served by starting with small stakes and putting the advantages of compounding and long-term horizons to work.

Just $5,000 is a great starting point for harnessing income from Altria stock. Image source: Getty Images.

With that in mind, the example of starting somewhat small with reliable dividend growth stocks, including tobacco behemoth Altria (MO +0.25%), is worth examining.

To be fair, $5,000 isn't a small amount of money, but it's not enough to retire on, either. However, it is a solid starting point for investors seeking a fair amount of income from Altria.

Here are the particulars on $5,000 worth of Altria shares. This Dividend King, or one of the companies with a dividend increase of at least 50 consecutive years, yields 5.8%, as of Thursday, Nov. 19. That's nearly 80 basis points above the yield on 10-year Treasuries. Based on the tobacco stock's closing price of $74.68 on Nov. 19, $5,000 buys 67 shares (I slightly rounded up there). Factor in the $4.44 per share annual dividend, and a $5,000 stake in Altria today generates nearly $297.50 in annual income.

That's not too shabby. Call it $300 and Altria's dividend, assuming it's not being reinvested, could cover a couple of months of phone bills or a nice dinner out. On the other hand, $300 isn't an earth-shattering amount of money, suggesting that investors should maintain perspective on Altria's income-generating capabilities.

That $300 in annual Altria payouts from a $5,000 stake is, well, today's figure. It doesn't account for dividend growth, something this consumer staples stock is a master of, as highlighted by its 57-year run of rising payouts. Put another way, investors buying Altria today get a $4.44-per-share annual dividend, but there's a solid chance that figure will be higher in 2027, 2028, and beyond.

Altria offers cash-strapped investors other reasons to get off the sidelines. Not only does the stock yield more than 10-year Treasuries, but its dividend yield is more than 5x that of the S&P 500.

Next, there's the matter of inflation. Take a leap of faith and assume/hope that the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes are enough to drive inflation down to the central bank's stated target of 2%. Or assume the worst and say that the Personal Consumer Expenditures (PCE) Price Index remains stuck at 3.6% as it read in September.

In either case, Altria's five- and 10-year dividend growth rates of 4.3% and 6.4%, respectively, vanquish inflation, and that's a good thing.

#3068. Is Netflix a Buy in November? The Bull and Bear Cases.

Netflix shares have fallen nearly 47% from their 52-week high. Is this a rare opportunity to buy a highly profitable entertainment business at a reasonable valuation?

By Lawrence Nga – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:15AM EST

Netflix (NFLX -2.96%) has had a difficult year. Its shares closed at $62.15 on Nov. 13, nearly 47% below their 52-week high. Yet the streaming giant continues to generate billions of dollars in revenue and profits. The sell-off raises an interesting question: Has Netflix become a bargain, or are investors right to worry about its future growth?

I cautiously lean toward the bull case. Netflix remains a highly profitable business with several ways to grow earnings over the next five years. However, its slowing growth and advertising challenges mean investors shouldn't expect an immediate recovery.

Netflix's ability to turn revenue into profits has improved over time.

In the third quarter of 2026, revenue increased 11.8% year over year to $12.87 billion. Operating income grew much faster, rising 37% to $4.46 billion. Its operating margin also improved to 34.6%, compared with 28.2% a year earlier.

In simple terms, Netflix is keeping more money from every dollar of revenue.

Management expects full-year revenue of $51.1 billion and operating income growth of more than 20% in 2026. It also expects its operating margin to reach 31.5%, up from 29.5% in 2025.

While operating leverage contributed to the expansion of operating margin, Netflix has also demonstrated pricing power. For instance, management said customers responded to its 2026 subscription price increases as expected, while customer cancellations improved year over year across every region.

Advertising offers another opportunity. Netflix expects advertising revenue to reach approximately $2.7 billion in 2026, despite delays in launching some advertising products. Management expects growth of more than 80% this year.

If Netflix can improve its advertising technology and earn more from its existing audience, advertising could become another meaningful contributor to future profits.

The biggest concern is that Netflix's growth is becoming harder to sustain. For perspective, revenue growth declined from 17.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 11.8% in the third quarter of 2026. Management expects 11.5% growth in the fourth quarter.

That's still healthy, but investors have become accustomed to high growth. As Netflix grows, attracting new customers and raising subscription prices become more challenging.

Competition is another concern. Alphabet’s YouTube and TikTok compete for people's attention, while Amazon and other streaming services continue investing in entertainment. Netflix must keep producing popular shows and films to remain relevant.

Management has acknowledged that its execution could improve, particularly in the United States. Recent changes to its content leadership suggest it wants to strengthen its entertainment offering.

Advertising is also taking longer to develop than expected. Netflix reduced its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from $3 billion to $2.7 billion because some advertising products were delayed in launching.

These problems don't threaten Netflix's business today. But they could limit how quickly it grows over the next several years.

While nobody likes a declining share price, Netflix's valuation has become much more reasonable as a result.

At $62.15, its market capitalization is approximately $255 billion. Its price-to-earnings (P/E ratio) is around 17.7 times, compared with a much higher valuation in previous years. For instance, the stock traded at a P/E ratio above 30 just a year ago.

If Netflix can sustain or even improve its growth rate from here on, the stock's valuation looks rather attractive at the current level. Of course, if growth continues to slow further, the opposite is true as well.

On balance, investors may consider buying Netflix at today's prices, particularly those with a five-year investment horizon. The company has improving profit margins, a global audience, and opportunities to grow its advertising business.

But I'd build a position gradually rather than invest everything at once. The next few quarters should reveal whether Netflix can maintain its profitability while stabilizing revenue growth and improving advertising execution.

Netflix doesn't need to return to its previous growth rates to reward shareholders. It simply needs to keep growing profits at a healthy pace.

The recently renovated Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort offers great views, a well-equipped fitness center and delicious food.

Hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

Room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

If you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

You can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

Make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.
